_comment: agent 站 52 份档案的正文首段（panel-lead）英文。2026-10-04 建；2026-10-08 A6.1 扩至 52 份。 2026-10-21 v8 T7：新增 chat/image/video/audio 14 条档案的键。
_note: 这些内容与 _onelines.en.json 的定位句高度重合（同一批作者写的位置说明），但用词更完整 —— 有的带官方引用与安全警告。**保留原文的强调与立场**：
_rules: 0) 保留 ** 强调（那是作者标注的「关键差别在哪」）。
1) 保留官方引用块的原文（英文引用不译，直接引）。
2) 保留安全警告的强度（明确标注 can reach local and internal IPs 这类不能软化）。
3) 产品名 / 参数 / 文档名原样（Aider in your IDE、npx、ACP、Atom feed）。
aider-cli: A terminal pair-programming tool where **Git integration is core design, not an add-on** — AI changes always live in version control, diffable and revertible.
aider: **Not an editor plugin but a usage mode** — Aider stays resident and watches your files; add an AI comment in any editor and it responds.
claude-code-cli: **The highest data quality and most frequent releases in this track** — it ships its own CHANGELOG and Atom feed, with the finest granularity in permission design.
claude-code: **One process, three entry points** — terminal, IDE and GitHub `@claude` mentions all share the same permission and context mechanism.
cline: **The only object here covering all three forms** — CLI, desktop app and VS Code extension share one open-source core, and the model is selectable.
codex-cli: OpenAI's official terminal coding agent, **written in Rust**, architecturally centred on the app server and thread resumption.
codex-ide: **The Codex IDE extension is an extension you install into VS Code / Cursor / Windsurf, not a standalone IDE** — it shares the same session mechanism with the CLI through the app server.
copilot: **The widest form coverage and the most GitHub-bound ecosystem** — website, CLI and mainstream editors, and it can delegate tasks to Claude / Codex (Preview).
crush:
**A TUI coding agent in the Charm ecosystem that runs in your terminal.**
Its MCP section is the most complete annotation of the three transports, and it ships an official subscription plan, Hyper.

Hyper is its own paid provider, so two cost models coexist. The license on GitHub is NOASSERTION, so commercial use is not something you can assume.
cursor: **One of the three most architecturally aggressive here**: a cloud agent that keeps running when you close the laptop, self-hosted code that never leaves the network, and code review split across two bots.
gemini-cli:
Google's official open-source terminal agent — npx, no install required.
Explicit MCP support, plus a non-interactive script mode.
grok-bot: **Of the three released at the same time, it is the only one whose official page lists the jobs.** It does not discuss mechanism — it just lists nine roles: sales leads, site building, inbox triage, meeting attendance and more.
meta-muse: **The only one that hands approval authority to another agent** — two system-isolated things run on the Muse Secure VM: Muse doing the work, and Sentinel able to veto it.
openai-dot: **Nothing installs locally; all work happens on OpenAI's cloud machine** — the stated capability boundary is blunt: a standalone cloud computer plus its own browser plus plugins into 4,000+ apps, and it keeps progressing after you shut down.
opencode: An MIT-licensed multi-provider programming harness that **asks permission before running bash commands**, and supports loading via ACP.
windsurf: **Now renamed Devin Desktop** (after the Cognition acquisition) — it has its own SWE-2 model, supports ACP preview, and has a CVE fix history involving Restricted Mode.
zed: **Not "yet another AI coding tool" but an orchestration layer for three agent paths** — use Zed's native agent in the same editor, or attach Claude / Codex / OpenCode / Copilot / Cursor.
claude-agent-sdk:
**What it is**: the Python programming interface to Claude Code. It turns a polished coding CLI into an object you can drive from Python. It is not a framework for building your own agent. **It is also the only coding base among our ten objects that cannot switch models** — every trade-off below follows from that.

> Official README, first line: "Python SDK for Claude Agent."
codex-sdk:
**"Turns the Codex CLI into an object you can drive inside a Node process"** — the official README opens with "Embed the Codex agent in your workflows and apps"; the second sentence settles the form:

> The TypeScript SDK **wraps** the `codex` CLI from `@openai/codex`.
> It **spawns the CLI** and exchanges JSONL events over stdin/stdout.
crewai:
**CrewAI is a Python framework that orchestrates multi-agent work through two metaphors: role division and business process.** The official description reads: "Framework for orchestrating **role-playing**, autonomous AI agents."

**The word "role-playing" makes people underrate it.** The same README also says production-grade, and promises plainly:

> "Move from experiment to production **without changing frameworks**."
deepagents: **Deep Agents is a general-purpose agent harness from LangChain.** It ships with filesystem, sub-agents, context management and skills already in place, so it runs out of the box. The official description is "batteries-included agent harness". It is built for long, multi-step tasks, and anything in that pre-bundled layer can be swapped without changing code. The security chapter states the agent follows a "trust the LLM" model and can do anything its tools allow; boundaries must be enforced at the tool/sandbox level, not by expecting the model to self-police. LangGraph is the graph runtime, LangChain's `create_agent` is a minimal harness on top of it, and Deep Agents is a more opinionated harness on top of `create_agent`.
google-adk:
**What it is, in one line**: Google ADK is a "code-first agent orchestration framework whose core asset is a graph execution engine". It organises several agents into one flow; it does not run a single agent for you.

The official README states its identity in the first feature it lists:

> **Workflow Runtime**: A graph-based execution engine for composing **deterministic execution flows** for agentic apps, with support for routing, fan-out/fan-in, **loops**, **retry**, **state management**, **dynamic nodes**, **human-in-the-loop**, and **nested workflows**.
hermes-agent:
**Hermes Agent is a resident cross-platform personal assistant that accumulates its own skills from experience.** It is not tied to your laptop — the official README says:

> **The self-improving AI agent** built by Nous Research.
> It's the only agent with a **built-in learning loop** — it creates skills from experience,
> improves them during use, **nudges itself to persist knowledge**, searches its own past
> conversations, and builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions.
> Run it on a $5 VPS, a GPU cluster, or serverless infrastructure that costs nearly nothing when idle.
> **It's not tied to your laptop** — talk to it from Telegram while it works on a cloud VM.

⚠ **This site's position on "the only agent"**: that is the **vendor's own marketing line**. This site **ran no cross-product comparison to test whether "only" holds**. It is recorded as a vendor claim, not as this site's conclusion.
langgraph:
**LangGraph is a low-level orchestration framework for building stateful agents.**

The official description is deliberately modest — note that word, low-level:

> Low-level orchestration framework for building **stateful** agents.

It does not claim to be a batteries-included high-level wrapper. It lays the groundwork for long-running, stateful work.
llamaindex:
**In one sentence**: LlamaIndex is a Python library. It pulls external data in for retrieval and question answering.

**⚠ But one thing has to be said first.**

The project has explicitly moved its company focus away from "orchestration frameworks":

> The **current focus** of LlamaIndex is to build the best AI-powered engine for
> **document parsing and extraction**. **LlamaParse** is our **enterprise platform** for
> agentic OCR, parsing, extraction, indexing and more.
>
> ...the company itself has undergone an **evolution** since when this OSS framework
> first launched 3 years ago in 2023.
>
> While we still have the OSS framework available as an open toolkit that you're welcome
> to use, **our primary focus has shifted towards LlamaParse**...

**The selection implication is direct.** The company's resources really have tilted towards document parsing, **but the orchestration capability has not left the OSS**:

- The README puts Workflows in the commercial-platform section (the link points at `cloud/llamaagents`)
- The official framework docs state that `llama-index-core` still ships a stable version of Workflows (checked 2026-10-08)

**What it actually provides now, the README itself lists best**:

> - **data connectors** to ingest your existing data sources and data formats (APIs, PDFs, docs, SQL, etc.)
> - ways to **structure your data** (indices, graphs)
> - an **advanced retrieval/query interface** over your data
> - easy **integrations with your outer application framework**

**Put together, the OSS framework now really provides five things**: data ingestion, indices / graph structures, a retrieval query interface, 300+ integrations, and Workflows orchestration.

**The value of this entry lies elsewhere** — it meets the v3 rule "a substantive update within 30 days" (pushed 2026-09-29, still active), but its real value is recording that turn honestly: behind 52,377★ the company is heading towards document parsing / agentic OCR, which is LlamaParse and ParseBench territory, not this open-source framework's.
openai-agents-sdk: **"A primitives-only multi-agent harness"** — the official description is "lightweight yet powerful": it hands you the agent-loop primitives and does not decide for you how the filesystem, planning or memory work.
openhands:
**It is a self-hosted control centre for agents** — the official README now calls it **Agent Canvas**.

It ships as a whole stack: a web GUI, a terminal UI, a CLI and a REST API all live in it. And it drives more than its own agent — Codex, Claude Code and Gemini can all run on top of it.

> Official positioning: The self-hosted developer control center for coding agents and automations.
> Run OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or **any ACP-compatible agent**
> across local, remote, and cloud backends.
context7: **The only remotely hosted entry in the MCP track** — version-aware library documentation for agents; MIT-licensed, but the core service lives on Upstash's side.
everything: **Not a usable tool** — the official page states plainly that this server exists for MCP client developers to run functional tests against; its only purpose is verifying that a client implements the protocol correctly.
fetch: A reference server that converts web pages to Markdown, **with an explicit security warning in its official README: it can reach local and internal IPs**.
filesystem: The file-operation implementation among MCP's official reference servers, **requiring allowed directories to be declared explicitly, with no silent whole-disk access**.
git: The version-control implementation among MCP's official reference servers, **scoped to a given git repository but with full local write capability**.
memory: A reference server implementing cross-session persistent memory with a local knowledge graph — **memory is written to disk, shared across sessions, with no access control**.
playwright: A browser automation server maintained by Microsoft, **driven by the accessibility tree rather than screenshots** — no vision model needed, and the output is a structured snapshot.
sequential-thinking: Provides a single `sequential_thinking` tool that lets an agent work through a complex problem **in a revisable, branchable way** — **it produces no intelligence, only structure**.
time: Does two things only: report the current time and convert time zones. **No files, no network — the lowest-risk category of server.**
ag2: AG2 is an open-source Python framework for building AI agents and coordinating multiple agents to solve tasks, with "agents capable of interacting with each other," broad LLM support, tooling, autonomous and human-in-the-loop workflows, and multi-agent conversation patterns. It is the community continuation of AutoGen: as of **v1.0** the protocol-driven framework became the top-level package (`import ag2`), while the classic framework (`ConversableAgent`, `GroupChat`, `import autogen`) moved to its own repository, `ag2ai/ag2-classic`. Officially, "AG2 v1.0 (`pip install ag2`) is **not** a drop-in upgrade from Classic. The agent model, orchestration, and imports all changed." v1.0 orchestrates agents through the **Network** — a `Hub` that owns the registry, write-ahead log, and audit trail, with agents talking over typed **channels** — and exposes an opt-in **harness** of composable primitives (`assembly=`, `knowledge=`, `tasks=`). It is licensed Apache-2.0 and runs entirely in your own process (no managed hosting), so the only cost is model calls, billed by whichever provider you install.
amp: Amp is Sourcegraph's frontier coding agent, spanning **CLI + cloud orbs + runners**. Send a prompt and you can close your laptop while it keeps working. It routes across frontier models, with the Oracle as a second-opinion model.
continue:
**An open-source IDE extension with fully self-configured models** — VS Code extension, JetBrains plugin and a `cn` CLI over one agent core, with models configured freely in `config.yaml`. The official model-provider list spans Anthropic, Azure AI Foundry, Amazon Bedrock, DeepSeek, Gemini, Mistral, **Ollama (local models)**, OpenAI, Vertex AI, xAI and "More (30 items)".

**The extension itself is free; the commercial line is a separate product.** The repository README states "Apache 2.0 © 2023-2026 Continue Dev, Inc." and there is no license fee for the extension — model calls are yours to pay (BYOK, or local Ollama). The commercial line is now **Continuous AI** at hub.continue.dev/pricing: Starter $3 / million tokens pay-as-you-go, Team $20 / seat / month (including $10 in credits per seat), Company custom (SAML/OIDC, BYOK, SLA).

**But the official status has changed.** Continue was acquired by Cursor; the homepage continue.dev now serves an acquisition notice, the old Hub pricing page `continue.dev/pricing` returns 404, and the repository is marked read-only. The last releases are the final 2.0.0 line for the VS Code extension, CLI and JetBrains plugin.
copilot-cli: GitHub Copilot CLI is the Copilot coding agent that runs in your terminal, carried by the same GitHub subscription as the IDE form factor. The official README says it is "Powered by the same agentic harness as GitHub's Copilot coding agent." Three things differ from the IDE form. It has a programmatic entry point (`copilot -p` / `--prompt`) that can go into scripts and CI. Approval is terminal-level: three choices on first use of a writing or executing tool, plus `--allow-all-tools` / `--allow-tool` / `--deny-tool` for unattended runs, and some official docs say denial wins. Billing is per prompt too: "Each time you submit a prompt to Copilot CLI, your monthly quota of Copilot premium requests is reduced by one."
cursor-cli:
**The terminal form of Cursor: it shares one account, one model catalogue and one `mcp.json` with the editor.**

The command is `agent`. Officially it supports "print automation for scripts and CI pipelines", so you can put the agent inside a script.

Against the IDE form it adds two paths. One is headless non-interactive use. The other is handing a session to a Cloud Agent or a persistent session.

Three differences from the IDE form: the interaction surface (a terminal), scriptability (`-p / --print` plus `--output-format text|json|stream-json`), and the way it plugs into other clients (`agent acp`, which serves ACP over stdio and JSON-RPC).
factory-droid: Factory AI's terminal coding agent. Its pitch is **model independence** — the official BYOK page says "Use your own OpenAI or Anthropic keys, connect to any open source model providers, or run models locally", and **your keys stay local: "Your API keys remain local and are not uploaded to Factory servers"**. Quota is not one monthly bucket but three independent rolling windows (5-hour / 7-day / 30-day); when you hit one you can fall back to **Droid Core** (a free open-weight model pool) or **Extra Usage** (prepaid credits, $10 minimum, never expiring). Every mutating action is gated by an **Autonomy Level** (Off / Low / Medium / High) plus command allow / deny / block lists. And it is not a single CLI: the official pricing page lists the Pro tier as "Factory App / Droid CLI / Droid SDK".
github-mcp:
GitHub's official MCP server (repository description: "GitHub's official MCP Server"). It connects any MCP client to GitHub's platform: reading repositories and code files, managing issues and PRs, monitoring Actions, inspecting code-scanning / Dependabot findings, and reading notifications.

**Two forms.** The **remote hosted** server (`https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, Streamable HTTP) is "hosted by GitHub and provides the easiest method for getting up and running... no local setup or runtime required." The **local** server runs as an stdio process via Docker (`ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server`) or a Go binary; GitHub Enterprise Server is only supported locally.

**Toolsets are the headline mechanism**: enable only what you need to help the LLM pick tools and shrink context. Default toolsets are `context, repos, issues, pull_requests, users`; 20+ groups exist in total, and the remote server adds extras (Copilot Spaces, Support Docs Search, `create_pull_request_with_copilot`).

**Two caution notes.** read-only mode is a "strict security filter" that takes precedence over everything else (write tools are skipped even if explicitly requested). Lockdown mode is explicitly "a best-effort content filter... **not** an authorization boundary."

Auth is OAuth (with scope challenges on the remote server) or a PAT (classic PATs get startup scope filtering; fine-grained PATs are not filtered). MIT licensed. Repository metadata (checked 2026-10-08): 33,446★, Go, latest release v2.0.2.
goose:
**A local-first, open-source general-purpose agent**: it runs as a desktop app, a full CLI and an embeddable API.

Created by Block and now hosted by the **Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation)**.

You can point it at Ollama or other local models, and its extension surface is built on MCP extensions.

**Stewardship note (checked 2026-10-08)**: this entry's collection started at the old repo address `github.com/block/goose`, which now redirects to `github.com/aaif-goose/goose`.

Official blog (2026-04-07): "Block has donated goose to the **Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)** at the Linux Foundation". README: "goose is part of the **Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)** at the Linux Foundation".

So this entry records the **current steward** Agentic AI Foundation in `vendor` — matching this site's convention of recording the current owner (as with Windsurf → Cognition). Block is the creator and stays credited in the body. `homepage` points at the **current canonical repository**, `github.com/aaif-goose/goose`, so no redirect address is collected.

The documentation site has also moved to `goose-docs.ai` (old docs links redirect).
jules: Google's asynchronous coding agent: point it at a GitHub repo, and it clones the code into a fresh cloud VM, plans the change, and opens a pull request for review. The difference from the IDE/CLI agents on this site is that the interaction is not live — you approve the plan and walk away. The official REST docs make the default explicit: "By default, sessions created through the API will have their plans automatically approved. If you want to create a session that requires explicit plan approval, set the `requirePlanApproval` field to `true`"; and "The `automationMode` field is optional. By default, no PR will be automatically created." Tiers are bundled, not sold separately: the GA post describes a free "Introductory access to Jules," "Jules in Google AI Pro: 5x higher limits" and "Jules in Google AI Ultra: 20x higher limits," noting that "Specific usage limits are listed at jules.google."
junie: Junie is JetBrains' coding agent, installed as a plugin — the official install page states "The Junie plugin is not bundled and not enabled in JetBrains IDEs by default" — and extended in March 2026 by a standalone Junie CLI for the terminal, any IDE, CI/CD and GitHub / GitLab. Its official framing is LLM-agnostic: "Junie supports all the top-performing models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Grok." On the IDE side it plans before it codes and, since GA, drives your IDE's real debugger rather than adding `println`.
kiro: Kiro is a desktop IDE — officially "a desktop development environment built on a VS Code foundation" — but it is framed as one agent, every surface: the IDE, CLI, Web and Mobile apps are all front ends to the same unified agent harness, connected over the open Agent Client Protocol (ACP). Its headline workflow is spec-driven development, turning a prompt into "requirements, architectural designs, and sequenced tasks", and its cloud sandbox sessions keep working "whether or not you're connected".
mastra:
Mastra is **a TypeScript framework for building AI agents and applications** - official README: "Mastra is a framework for building AI-powered applications and agents with a **modern TypeScript stack**. It includes **everything you need** to go from early prototypes to production-ready applications."

One package covers Agents, graph Workflows, Memory, RAG, Evals/Scorers, MCP client and server, a built-in Hono server, Studio and observability.

**Model routing is where it goes furthest**: `provider/model` strings, plus model fallbacks, per-task mix-and-match and `requestContext`.

**State is separate from context**: workflow snapshots persist across deployments and restarts, while memory covers message history, Observational Memory, working memory and semantic recall.

**The licence splits in two** - the core framework is Apache-2.0, but code under any `ee/` directory is source-available under the Mastra Enterprise License (the repo licence API returns NOASSERTION). Studio, Observability and hosted deployment are Mastra platform products, billed on Starter $0 / Teams $250 / Enterprise tiers.
microsoft-agent-framework: **What it is**: "the Microsoft-official agent foundation that merged Semantic Kernel and AutoGen". Full name **Microsoft Agent Framework** (MAF below). The official announcement page puts the lineage most plainly — "Microsoft Agent Framework **doesn't replace** Semantic Kernel and AutoGen — it **builds on them**" — and the official overview is just as direct: "It brings together and extends ideas from **Semantic Kernel and AutoGen** projects... Built by the same teams, it is the **unified foundation** for building AI agents going forward." One thing is enough to remember: **it is not "yet another new framework" — Microsoft folded two product lines into one.**
pydantic-ai: **Pydantic AI is the Python agent library from Pydantic.** Its selling point is type safety. The official self-description puts two keywords together: "**Pydantic AI** is the Python AI SDK: a **typed**, extensible **agent loop** with every model a string swap away." "Typed" is its worldview: Pydantic runs natively from the data layer all the way to agent output. "Agent loop" is its shape: it hands you primitives, not a finished product. It sits in the same bracket as the OpenAI Agents SDK, but goes noticeably deeper on two points — type safety and durable execution.
smolagents:
A thin agent library from Hugging Face — the repository description is literal: "**barebones library for agents that think in code**".

**The core difference is code-as-action.** The default `CodeAgent` lets the LLM write its actions as Python code and execute them, instead of emitting JSON tool calls. The official claim is that this "uses **30% fewer steps**" and reaches higher scores on difficult benchmarks (README cites arXiv 2402.01030 / 2411.01747). A `ToolCallingAgent` that emits JSON is also provided, officially positioned for scenarios that favour reliability and structured validation — either one works.

**Model-agnostic by design.** Several Model classes, one per route: `InferenceClientModel` on the Hub's Inference Providers, plus `LiteLLMModel` ("100+ different models"), `OpenAIModel`, `AzureOpenAIModel`, `AmazonBedrockModel`, and locally `TransformersModel` / `MLXModel` / `Ollama`. Swapping provider means swapping a Model class.

**On safety the docs are blunt.** The default `LocalPythonExecutor` is not a security sandbox — README states it "is **not** a security sandbox. It applies some restrictions but can be bypassed and must not be used as a security boundary." Real isolation requires a remote sandbox: Blaxel, E2B, Modal or Docker.
warp: Warp is an open-source **Agentic Development Environment** — the vendor's own wording, verbatim. The same **Warp Agent** is reachable three ways: "In the Warp app", "In any terminal, with the Warp Agent CLI", and "In the cloud, as a cloud agent". Account, rules, skills and model access are shared across all three. The CLI is "a standalone terminal program that runs the Warp Agent" and "a native terminal multiplexer" with its own PTY, so it runs in any terminal emulator, **including over SSH**. Every proposed action is checked against an execution profile whose values are `agent_decides` / `always_ask` / `always_allow`; file edits are `agent_decides` by default but still prompt every time, so "you always review a diff before it's applied".
chatgpt: The industry definer of general-purpose chat assistants: web, apps and desktop fully covered, model family split by subscription tier — and the data-training toggle is its most commonly misread clause.
claude-chat: A general chat app strong on long-form and writing quality: memory is an editable per-item list, and the Cowork line put “pause and resume after shutdown, scheduled tasks” into official release notes.
gemini-chat: The general chat assistant inside the Google ecosystem: web, Windows and macOS covered, models split by subscription tier — “it won't train on your raw Gmail/Drive, but it does train on summaries produced while answering” is its most easily misread clause.
grok-chat: The general chat assistant wired into X's live information: search and public-post retrieval are the core differentiators — “logged-out users may get no training opt-out option” and “inside X a different set of terms applies” are the two boundaries to check first.
kimi-chat: The workhorse for long Chinese-document chat: the K3/K2.7 Code/K2.6/K2.5 model family is a clear official product line — “opting out of training goes through customer-service registration, at account level” is the process to confirm in advance.
doubao-chat: The domestic workhorse for everyday Chinese Q&A and text-to-image: the App training toggle is self-serve — “App may train by default, API doesn't train by default” is the opposite-direction pair of clauses most easily mixed up.
midjourney: The industry benchmark for image-generation style quality: web + Discord dual line, community output public and Remixable by default; “paid users own the Assets, but high-revenue companies need a higher tier” is the licensing threshold most overlooked.
stability-ai: The image vendor on the “platform + open weights” dual route: the platform assigns output ownership to users and the training opt-out is written into the terms; self-hosting the open-weights line commercially requires checking each model's license.
flux: The dual-route supplier of the FLUX model family: hosted generation via the official API/playground, some weights open for self-hosting and even on-device; “claims no ownership, but bans training other models” is the sharpest cut in the terms.
veo: Google's video-generation model family: delivered via the Gemini API / Vertex AI and Google AI plans, with SynthID provenance; “free-quota content is trained on, paid is not” is the watershed in the data clauses.
runway: A leading video-generation creation platform: its own Gen models plus third-party model aggregation, with MCP and editing-software plugins fully rolled out; “the training license is irrevocable with no opt-out switch” is the hardest clause in the data terms.
kling: The domestic video-generation leader: Kling 4.0 does a native 30-second single pass and Omni-Reference takes 15 material inputs, it is filed and directly accessible from mainland China; “ownership belongs to the user, but commercial use requires the membership tier” is the key licensing split.
suno: The AI-music generation leader: songs, vocals, Voice Models and the Suno Studio workstation; “commercial use is tied to the paid-download quota, Remix is always non-commercial” is the most concrete licensing split in the terms.
elevenlabs: The broadest product surface in speech synthesis and voiceover: TTS, cloning, transcription, conversational AI and workflow orchestration in one place; “the training opt-out is a self-serve menu” is rare among peers, and commercial rights are tier-bound.
n8n: **n8n is an automation-first low-code workflow platform** — AI is one node type among many, not its identity. The most misread part is the license: source is public, but it is **fair-code (Sustainable Use License)**, not OSI open source.
dify: **Dify is the China-origin, globally-facing agentic workflow platform**: prompt logic becomes visible, testable, handoff-ready Workflow/Chatflow execution paths, with knowledge pipelines and Marketplace integrations as first-class citizens. The license is “Apache 2.0 + two additional conditions” — the multi-tenant restriction is the first thing to read.
coze: **Coze is ByteDance's cloud-hosted agent-building platform**: the domestic edition leads with “free model switching + always-on cloud phone/cloud PC + direct distribution via WeChat/Douyin/Feishu”; coze.com is the same product's other entry. There is no self-hosted form — data and runtime live in the cloud.
zapier: **Zapier is the synonym for the connector ecosystem** — a cloud-hosted automation platform with 6000+ SaaS integrations, whose official narrative now puts AI/agents (Canvas, Agents) at the main axis. No self-hosted form; everything runs in the cloud.
make: **Make (formerly Integromat) is the flowchart school of visual automation** — branches, iterations and routers read more directly on the canvas than the form school; AI is one module among many, automation is the identity. Pure cloud hosting, no self-hosting.
activepieces: **Activepieces is the cleanest-license tier of open-source low-code automation**: MIT Expat for the main body, only the ee/ directory is the commercial-license zone — looser than n8n's SUL, at the cost of a much smaller connector catalog. Self-hosted + official cloud, two lines.
flowise: **Flowise is the founding generation of “build LLM apps on a canvas”** (a visual wrapper over LangChain components): RAG/agent-flow prototyping is extremely fast. Two honest notes: the license is Apache 2.0 + an enterprise commercial zone; repo pushes slowed after 2026-08 — momentum is a snapshot fact.
langflow: **Langflow is the largest LLM canvas with the cleanest license (whole-repo MIT)**, now under DataStax — the product narrative tilts toward the enterprise data stack (AstraDB vector line). Python custom components are its extension axis.
pipedream: **Pipedream is the developer-facing automation platform**: code steps (Node/Python/Bash) are first-class citizens, the UI is a flow-building shell; the Connect line makes *your app* a node inside other people's workflows — being integrated is its commercial axis.
copilot-studio: **Copilot Studio is Microsoft's enterprise low-code agent platform** — whether it is usable largely depends on whether you are inside the Power Platform/Dataverse ecosystem. Enterprise governance (identity, data residency) comes ready-made with the Microsoft 365 system.
vertex-agent-builder: **Vertex AI Agent Builder is Google's enterprise agent platform line** — the official page now sits under the “Gemini platform” narrative (build/deploy/govern enterprise-ready agents). It is the other leg of the same strategy as the code-side Google ADK.
bedrock-agents: **The Bedrock agent line is AWS's hosted agent platform**: Agents (visual orchestration) + AgentCore (framework-agnostic hosted runtime), two lines. One URL fact: the old entry bedrock/agent/ is now 404 (direct-fetched 2026-10-21) — current entries are agents/ and agentcore/.
agentforce: **Agentforce is Salesforce's in-ecosystem enterprise agent platform** — its value anchor is CRM records and Data Cloud as natural context: “the agent knows everything about the customer” in service/sales scenarios is a structural advantage general platforms cannot give. Outside the Salesforce ecosystem, the anchor disappears.
relevance-ai: **Relevance AI leads with “build an AI workforce with no code”** — multi-agent collaboration is its narrative axis, sales/operations automation is the main battlefield. Cloud-hosted, no self-hosting.
ollama: **Ollama is the de-facto entry point for running open models locally**: one command installs it, the official model library pulls models in one click, and an OpenAI-compatible API comes up on your machine. Honest notes: the tool is MIT but weight licenses follow each model; the official README explicitly mentions a cloud line.
lm-studio: **LM Studio is the mainstream graphical entry for local models on the desktop**: in-app model downloads, dual runtimes (MLX + llama.cpp), built-in local server. 2026-10 snapshot: the site now leads with Bionic — a local-agent narrative that overshadows plain chat. Honest notes: the app is closed-source; the terms page loads dynamically and could not be direct-fetched.
llama-cpp: **llama.cpp is the bedrock of the entire local-inference ecosystem**: GGUF is defined here, the models-site quant index is built to its yardstick, and Ollama/LM Studio/KoboldCpp all build on top of it. MIT, pure C/C++, with an official REST line via llama-server.
vllm: **vLLM is the benchmark for serving open models**: PagedAttention makes memory management its core strength, and the OpenAI-compatible server plugs straight into existing clients. Apache-2.0, PyTorch Foundation umbrella. Numbers: vendor-claimed performance figures live in the models-site guides snapshot; this site does not benchmark.
sglang: **SGLang is the prefix-reuse generation of serving engines**: RadixAttention makes KV-cache reuse across turns and shared prefixes the main axis, so agent workloads benefit directly. Apache-2.0, LMSYS-line academic open source. Vendor figures follow the models-site guides snapshot.
jan: **Jan is the long-standing open-source 'offline ChatGPT replacement'**: 100% offline local models, Apache-2.0 core plus an attribution request. Honest notes: the GitHub API's NOASSERTION flag comes from that extra sentence — read the LICENSE itself; the site measured 000 direct (network-limited, not dead).
gpt4all: **GPT4All is the founding standard-bearer of 'local models on everyone's device'** (Nomic AI, MIT): CPU-first, desktop out of the box, commercial use with no strings. Honest note: last push 2025-05-27 (API snapshot) — the stars are history, check the current maintenance cadence.
mlx: **MLX is Apple's official local-inference stack for Apple silicon**: a native framework for unified memory (mlx) plus the official LLM layer (mlx-lm), MIT, actively maintained. The 'native son' route for Mac users — even fine-tuning lives in the same stack.
koboldcpp: **KoboldCpp is the veteran local runner of the roleplay/creative-writing scene**: single-file zero-install, GGUF, the Kobold context-management tradition. AGPL-3.0 — read the copyleft obligations before commercial integration. Honest note: the official repo lives under LostRuins (the koboldai path 404s).
text-generation-webui: **text-generation-webui (now renamed textgen) is the Swiss-army generation of local LLMs**: multi-loader, an extension ecosystem, the richest community playstyles. Honest notes: the repo is now oobabooga/textgen; last push 2026-08-17 (API snapshot) — maintenance sits between active and slowing.
tgi: **TGI is Hugging Face's official serving-inference server**: weights, clients and docs in one ecosystem, Apache-2.0. Honest note: last push 2026-03-21 (API snapshot) — current serving heat is with vLLM/SGLang; check the cadence before choosing.
localai: **LocalAI is the 'change the URL and go local' multimodal runtime**: a single OpenAI-compatible binary fronting multiple engines, with text/voice/vision/agent workloads on one stack. MIT, actively maintained (v4.8.0 per the official site).
sentry-mcp: **Sentry's official agent tooling line**: crashes, events and releases wrapped as MCP tools, so a coding agent can ask 'is this error live?'. Honest notes: the old sentry-mcp repo now redirects to getsentry/toolkit; the license is FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0 — not plain Apache, production use has a restriction window.
notion-mcp: **Notion's own MCP server**: fully hosted (mcp.notion.com/mcp) — agents search the workspace and read/write pages and databases. One line matters: **the agent's visibility equals the page permissions of the account you connect**.
slack-mcp: **Slack's self-hosted official MCP server** (mcp.slack.com/mcp): agents search the workspace, read threads, draft messages, manage canvases and Lists. Two hard facts: **admin approval is a front gate**; it only answers inside a session — no watching, no triggers. The old slackapi repo 404s; the reference version was archived to a third party.
supabase-mcp: **Supabase's official MCP server** (Apache-2.0, repo now supabase/mcp): agents inspect schema, run migrations, read logs. Security in one line: **its SQL execution surface is real — defend as if it can change your database; tool trimming is not a sandbox**.
stripe-mcp: **Stripe's official agent tooling line** (stripe/ai, MIT): look up API usage, query account objects, rehearse in test mode. Two clarifications: it is not the agentic-commerce (ACP payments) product line; and **write tools (refunds/invoices) exist — defend against the worst case of your key's permissions**.
chrome-devtools-mcp: **Chrome's own team built 'let the agent see the browser'**: direct CDP — navigate, interact, screenshot, performance traces, network and console. Apache-2.0, 53k stars, active. Security in one line: **it drives a real browser with a real network exit, and the server itself has no URL allowlist layer**.
figma-mcp: **Figma's official MCP server**: design-system context (components/variables/Code Connect) fed to coding agents, plus canvas writes. Three hard facts: **the remote server is the officially recommended form**; **only clients in the Figma MCP catalog can connect**; **beta-free is temporary — usage-based pricing is coming**.
linear-mcp: **Linear's official MCP server** (mcp.linear.app/mcp): agents search, create and update issues. One direct-fetched fact: **the old SSE endpoint is gone** — configs still pointing at /sse need to switch to /mcp.
mongodb-mcp: **MongoDB's official MCP server** (mongodb-js repo, Apache-2.0): agents connect to databases, query collections, run aggregations, write data, manage Atlas. Honest note: the docs/mcp path 404s — the live official line is the GitHub repo. **Delete tools carry confirmation parameters, but confirmation is not a sandbox — credentials are the boundary**.
cloudflare-mcp: **Cloudflare's official MCP server** (Apache-2.0): agents write Workers, deploy, manage D1/R2/DNS, search official docs. It has **the finest restricted-token granularity in its class** — but remember 'can deploy = can run arbitrary code'; scope tokens to the minimum.
atlassian-mcp: **Atlassian's official Remote MCP server**: one endpoint covers Jira + Confluence — agents search requirements, create issues, write wiki pages. OAuth 3LO user auth; visibility follows account permissions.
zapier-mcp: **Zapier MCP is an entry point to a thousand apps**: whatever actions you tick in Zapier's config become the agent's tools — the tool surface is allowlist-generated, not vendor-preset. That structure is itself a tightening measure: unticked means nonexistent.
brave-search-mcp: **Brave's official search MCP server** (MIT): an independent retrieval source for agents (web/news/images/places). One archival fact: the old Brave reference in the MCP org repo was archived, and the official README says the @brave package replaces it — this profile is the live one.
neon-mcp: **Neon's official MCP server** (MIT): agents manage Neon projects, create branches, run SQL. The signature is **the branch model** — agents can try changes on a copy; but the default connection surface is unchanged, so defend as if it can execute SQL and the management key can delete projects.
langchain: **LangChain is the main body of the LLM-app framework ecosystem** (MIT, 148k stars): a unified abstraction layer for models/tools/retrieval with the largest integration surface on the web. Three lines from the same vendor to keep apart: LangChain (component abstraction), LangGraph (graph orchestration), Deep Agents (prebuilt deep agents).
dspy: **DSPy turns 'tuning prompts' into a programming problem** (MIT, Stanford NLP/Databricks): signatures declare inputs/outputs, optimizers train prompts as parameters. The dividing line in one sentence: **do you have an evaluation metric** — with one it is a lever, without one it has nothing to optimize.
haystack: **Haystack is the RAG framework of the 'retrieval-quality engineering' school** (Apache-2.0, deepset): separated indexing/query pipelines, hybrid retrieval with rerankers, an evaluation loop — the most production-flavored RAG line. The 2.x pipeline API was rewritten; beware old tutorials.
agentscope: **AgentScope is the flagship domestic multi-agent framework** (Apache-2.0, Alibaba/ModelScope line): a clean Msg message-passing abstraction, with a visual Studio workbench and distributed-execution lines. 33k stars, actively maintained. Per rule L5: all capability descriptions paraphrase official docs.
strands-agents: **AWS's open-source agent SDK** (Apache-2.0): model-driven loops, decorator-style tools, **MCP client support on the official mainline**. Keep it apart from the hosted Bedrock Agents line: Strands is a build-it-yourself foundation (this category); the hosted line lives in automation. The repo is now harness-sdk (old name redirects — direct-fetched).
swe-agent: **SWE-agent is the benchmark harness of the 'agents fix code' research line** (MIT, Princeton/Stanford): ACI (agent-computer interface) is its core thesis, co-origin with the SWE-bench evaluation ecosystem. Production out-of-the-box is not its positioning — it is a reference implementation for research and evaluation.
letta: **Letta (formerly MemGPT) makes agents persistent entities** (Apache-2.0): a resident agent server, layered memory (self-edited core + retrieval-backed archival), sessions that interrupt and resume. Form is its biggest difference from other frameworks — **it is a server, not a library**.
devin: **Devin is the 'ticket in, draft PR out' cloud async software engineer** (Cognition): sessions run in the vendor's cloud workspace with its own shell/IDE/browser trio, dispatch work straight from Slack/Linear/Jira, and grind through backlogs in parallel.
replit-agent: **Replit Agent is the cloud-IDE agent from plain language to a deployable app**: it builds the project, sets up infrastructure, tests, and deploys in one chain; Free/Power/Max modes pick tiers rather than bare models, with checkpoints as the rollback safety net.
codebuddy: **CodeBuddy is Tencent Cloud's three-surface coding assistant** (plugin / AI IDE / CLI): Hunyuan as the anchor with other LLMs pluggable, Figma-to-code and one-click CloudStudio deploys; the Hunyuan model's filing number is published in the official docs.
google-antigravity: **Google Antigravity is Google's agent-first development platform**: desktop command center / CLI / IDE extensions / Python SDK — four surfaces on one harness, with command-execution policy and workspace boundaries as three explicit control switches in the official docs.
trae: **Trae is ByteDance's three-client AI IDE** (desktop / web / mobile): dual windows on desktop (Agent/IDE) with SOLO mode for whole-task delegation, built-in multi-model plus custom keys, Privacy mode and sandboxed execution as official switches.
deepseek-chat: **DeepSeek is the domestic chat product built on reasoning-first Q&A with traceable official model docs**: cloud chat and API docs share one family, open-weight models are selectable off-site; the filing number is cross-verified on two cloud vendors' official disclosure pages.
yuanbao-chat: **Tencent Yuanbao is the general AI assistant living in the WeChat ecosystem**: search official accounts/Channels, @-mention it in comment sections, integrate Tencent Docs and WeChat Read; long-document reading is its strong suit, powered by Tencent's self-developed Hunyuan (Hy) models.
chatglm-chat: **Zhipu Qingyan (ChatGLM) is the domestic chat product built on long-document parsing plus knowledge-base retrieval**: GLM open weights make local runs a same-family option; first-batch filed (2023-08-31); product/model names overlap — relay per the official pages' subjects.
tongyi-qianwen: **Tongyi Qianwen is Alibaba's consumer entry to the Qwen family**: multimodal understanding + document parsing, Qwen open weights runnable locally; the filing number is verified on Alibaba Cloud's official disclosure page. Don't mix the vendor's three lines — Qwen chat / Wanxiang image-video / Bailian API.
wenxin: **Wenxin is Baidu's ecosystem chat entry** (Search/Wenku/Netdisk integration + web search): the ERNIE line keeps weights closed, first-batch filed (2023-08-31); the rename history 'Wenxin Yiyan → Wenxiaoyan → Wenxin' is the easiest retrieval trap.
microsoft-copilot: **Microsoft Copilot is the free chat entry of the Windows/Edge/Bing ecosystem**: web search is the base capability, models are routed on Microsoft's side; it is three different products from Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot — don't mix them.
manus: **Manus is the general-task agent you hand whole tasks to in a cloud sandbox**: code execution/browsing/output/publishing (manus.space) run in a cloud VM, models are orchestrated by the product with no user selection; credits-based, async is its core form.
xinghuo-spark: **iFlytek Spark is the domestic chat product with a strong voice foundation** (iFlytek's self-developed Spark series; recognition/synthesis/interpretation are traditional strengths): education/office friendly, first-batch filed (2023-08-23); the Spark line does not open its weights.
jimeng: **Jimeng is ByteDance's dedicated image/video creation console** (Seedream/Seedance model lines, built by the Jianying team): text-to-image, image-to-video and digital-human lines in one console; the generative-AI service filing number was not found (only an ICP number verified) — filing: unknown is an honest gap, not a verdict.
tongyi-wanxiang: **Tongyi Wanxiang is Alibaba's image/video creation console with an open-weights twin**: the Wan weight family is Apache-2.0 (verified via GitHub API), runnable locally; the cloud console carries filing number Shanghai-TongYiWanXiang-202410090024.
ideogram: **Ideogram is the typography-first image generator** (text rendering inside images is its signature): 4.0 released open quantized weights (free but non-commercial), 4.5 is closed; direct access from the mainland measures 000.
recraft: **Recraft is the rare vector-native design console**: true SVG output, brand-kit consistency, precise in-image text placement; free-plan works are public and not licensed for commercial use — the plan-level hard line.
adobe-firefly: **Adobe Firefly is the enterprise-grade design AI line** (standalone product, not the generation-fill inside Photoshop): licensed-training + enterprise indemnification narrative; third-party models selectable inside the app per official positioning.
microsoft-designer: **Microsoft Designer is the free design entry of the Microsoft ecosystem** (templates + generation): models routed on Microsoft's side; same ecosystem as Copilot's image line but a different entry; commercial rights vary by subscription tier.
leonardo-ai: **Leonardo is the game-asset-oriented image console**: self-developed Phoenix/Lucid lines + Element few-shot training for style/character consistency + a model hub; under Canva since July 2024.
krea: **Krea is the real-time + multi-model aggregation console**: draw-as-you-see realtime line is the signature, 64+ third-party models aggregated (Veo/Ideogram/Flux…) plus self-developed Krea 2; 'Do not train' is marketing copy, terms govern.
seaart: **SeaArt is the community-type anime/illustration aggregation console**: cloud LoRA training with ComfyUI export, a community model library whose licenses are labeled per model, multi-vendor model aggregation; a going-overseas product by Chengdu-based Haiyi.
clipdrop: **Clipdrop is the single-image atomic-operation toolkit**: cutout/cleanup/relight (its signature)/upscale/uncrop each as a standalone tool; ownership moved three times (InitML→Stability→Jasper, Feb 2024) — API terms now run on Jasper's side.
hailuo-video: **Hailuo Video is MiniMax's consumer video entry** (self-developed line; text/image-to-video as main functions): domestic, direct-connect usable, free tier to start; the filing number is model-level (Shanghai-MiniMax-202505230046) — the product entry's own filing status was not separately verified.
vidu: **Vidu is the Tsinghua-linked Shengshu Technology's video model entry**: its signature is reference-to-video with multi-subject consistency — for narrative/animation work that needs character consistency, it's the one domestic player leaning hardest on that.
pixverse: **PixVerse is Aishi Technology's video entry**: effect templates/playfulness are the community grip, the R-series 'general real-time world model' bets on interactive generation; among domestic players it iterates fastest.
pika: **Pika is the social-effect video entry**: Pikaffects exaggerated physical effects are the memory point — the product centers on playfulness, not film-grade generation; mainland direct access measures 000.
luma: **Luma's Dream Machine leads with camera-motion short video**: first/last-frame interpolation and camerawork narrative are the signature; the company also keeps a 3D/NeRF capture line; mainland direct access measures 000.
higgsfield: **Higgsfield turns camera moves into a product**: preset camera language (dolly/crash zoom/crane…) applied to generated video in one click — it sells 'directorial feel', not a general generator.
heygen: **HeyGen is the digital-human video console**: Avatar + Voice + Translation, leading with enterprise video localization (translation + lip-sync) and consented cloned presenters; it generates 'people talking', not 'worlds'.
synthesia: **Synthesia is the enterprise-training digital-human console**: L&D/compliance training/multilingual localization are the lead scenarios, SCORM integration is the moat; a subscription-first product posture.
d-id: **D-ID makes photos talk**: Talking Photo is the signature + real-time interactive Agents line + an API-first integration surface; lightweight photo-driven, not high-fidelity cloning.
udio: **Udio is the other half of the music-generation duo** (v1.5 Allegro line, complex-genre reputation), now mid-transition from copyright defendant to licensed platform — UMG/WMG have settled, the new platform goes walled-garden.
minimax-audio: **MiniMax Audio is the domestic TTS/voice-clone/API three-in-one audio line**: strong Chinese speech quality + voice cloning + music models served via API; web and API are two entries with two sets of terms.
whisper: **Whisper is the open-source base of transcription**: MIT weights in multiple sizes run locally, privacy-sensitive audio never leaves the machine; it's a model, not a product — meeting-note UX needs a shell, diarization needs derivative tooling.
fish-audio: **fish audio is the zero-shot voice-clone TTS console**: upload a sample and the voice is cloned + a community voice market; between 'it works' and 'it's compliant' sits the consent red line.
deepgram: **Deepgram is the developer-facing speech API platform**: Nova transcription + Aura TTS, real-time streaming is the lead; it's the base for building speech products, not an end-user transcription product.
assemblyai: **AssemblyAI is the 'transcription + understanding' speech API**: summarization/entities/Q&A on top of transcripts (the LeMUR line); documentation experience is its developer reputation — offset competition with Deepgram's real-time performance narrative.
otter: **Otter is the bot-joins-the-meeting transcription & notes product**: real-time transcription + action items + cross-meeting Q&A, mature for English; the bot entering your meeting is itself a compliance question.
moyin: **Moyin Workshop is Mobvoi's Chinese dubbing workbench**: multi-voice text-to-speech + voice cloning + video-dubbing workflows, algorithm filing on record; domestic direct access and Chinese support are its convenience surface.
perplexity: The flagship of "answers with source footnotes" AI search: multi-model routing plus an in-house line; the Comet browser extends search into agentic browsing — but the original behind each footnote still needs your own check.
notebooklm: A source-anchored research workbench: you hand it a set of sources and it answers only inside them, plus audio overviews and study guides — it is not a search engine but a Q&A engine over your material.
elicit: An academic-literature "retrieve + structured extraction" workbench: research question → paper screening → extraction tables → cited synthesis — a systematic-review pipeline, AI-assisted; every cell still needs checking against the original.
metaso: The Chinese AI search that "skips ads, goes straight to results": in-house MetaLLM (a rare self-built route), six retrieval lanes, Chinese academic databases, outline/mind-map structured output; reachable directly from the mainland.
genspark: A research agent doing "search → report → slides" end to end: Sparkpage reorganizes retrieval results, Slides/Sheets/websites come out as finished artifacts — an agent form means accepting some process opacity.
kagi: A self-built-index search engine where you pay for privacy: no ads and no tracking is the main axis, the AI answer layer (FastGPT/Teclis) is the add-on — the exact reverse order of "AI search".
you-com: You.com has shifted its center of gravity from consumer AI search to enterprise retrieval infrastructure (ARI/Research API): the consumer answer engine still runs, but list "consumer longevity" as a risk when choosing.
consensus: Consensus answers "what does the scientific literature say": the Consensus Meter tallies conclusion polarity across studies into a summary — a fast read on empirical consensus, but the count is unweighted and the Meter is not a verdict.
tiangong: Tiangong grew from "AI search" into a "super agent": search as the base, with documents/PPT/spreadsheets/webpages generated directly in multiple modes, plus template reuse ("make the same"); reachable directly from the mainland.
devv: A developer-facing AI search Q&A: coding questions → live fetch of official docs → answers with links; it answers code questions but does not touch your codebase — that is the boundary with the coding category.
andi: Andi takes the "generate the answer directly" AI-native search route: not retrieve-then-wrap but a self-built architecture answering directly with sources, free and ad-free with a no-tracking privacy narrative — a small-team product whose longevity is a risk item.
qoder-cn: **Qoder CN is Alibaba Cloud's AI coding product line** (formerly Lingma, officially renamed 2026-05-20): desktop IDE + JetBrains plugin + CLI, switchable mainstream domestic models or BYOK, three context layers (memory / Repo Wiki / knowledge base), Credits shared across the family — 'first-party Alibaba Cloud product + domestic deployment' is its official compliance narrative.
lovable: **Lovable is Sweden's full-stack AI app builder**: natural language in, a working app out with frontend, database, auth and hosting — the built-in backend runs on the Supabase open-source foundation, Git two-way sync puts code in your own repo, and the official line is 'never locked in'. But you cannot pick the build model, and the training-data policy splits by plan.
bolt-new: **Bolt.new is StackBlitz's in-browser full-stack AI builder**: it runs on WebContainers (Node.js directly in the browser, no local setup), the agent comes in Standard and Max tiers billed by tokens, Bolt Cloud adds hosting plus a database, and a GitHub sync line is in place.
v0: **v0 is Vercel's prompt-to-full-stack platform**: chats generate Next.js apps, a VM sandbox runs a real terminal with pre-installed agents (claude is ready to use), GitHub sync moves code into your repo, and publishing runs through the Vercel deployment chain — Ask/Auto/Full permission tiers, custom models are Enterprise-side.
